headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors via shared MCP/file workflows; data leakage and compliance risks are moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write runtime files and use MCP, while OpenMetadata exposes MCP/stdio plus APIs/webhooks. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if OpenMetadata outputs are fed into OpenHands through shared files or MCP, even though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata output is written into a file or MCP message that OpenHands later parses as instructions, injection becomes active.
IF both agents are connected through the same MCP server or mounted volume, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces.
Disable automatic instruction-following on imported files.
Require provenance tags on MCP/file inputs.
Review any shared MCP server configuration.
requires-engineering: add content sanitization and allowlist parsing for inter-agent messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches mounted runtime files and handles model provider API keys; OpenMetadata touches technical metadata, lineage, governance, and memory/tribal knowledge. If they share a mounted workspace or metadata store, sensitive operational data can flow from A into B outputs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace by default, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted volume or metadata repository, A's files can be exposed to B.
IF OpenMetadata exports lineage or governance records containing secrets into APIs/webhooks, those records can be surfaced in B outputs.
mitigations: Use separate storage roots for each agent.
Remove secrets from shared files before ingestion.
Restrict OpenMetadata API/webhook payloads to non-sensitive fields.
Rotate any API keys present in the OpenHands runtime.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls and redaction at the integration layer.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has broad write and git-modifying capabilities; OpenMetadata is runnable and uses MCP/APIs/webhooks, implying it can also mutate shared resources through integrations. If both target the same repo, dataset, or metadata backend, concurrent writes can conflict. The profiles do not show explicit locking, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same git repository or filesystem path, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF both agents mutate the same metadata backend through APIs or webhooks, last-write-wins conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint write targets.
Pause one agent during commits or schema changes.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Add a manual merge checkpoint before writes land.
requires-engineering: implement locking or optimistic concurrency on shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, shell actions, and browser-derived outputs; OpenMetadata can consume and publish metadata, lineage, and governance information. If OpenMetadata treats OpenHands output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect catalog entries or downstream actions. No verification step is documented, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata ingests OpenHands-produced facts without validation, incorrect metadata can propagate.
IF OpenHands writes generated artifacts that OpenMetadata republishes, downstream consumers may act on unverified content.
mitigations: Require human review before publishing shared outputs.
Cross-check generated facts against source systems.
Mark OpenHands outputs as untrusted by default.
Limit OpenMetadata publication to validated records.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates between generation and catalog publication.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, but OpenHands explicitly handles model provider API keys and runtime files, while OpenMetadata touches governance and memory/tribal knowledge. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a small compliance gap is evidenced. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their interaction, not a single-agent violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared runtime or metadata store, retention and access controls must be checked.
IF OpenMetadata is configured to retain governance records longer than the OpenHands runtime, retention mismatch becomes material.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared pair.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Disable unnecessary logging on both sides.
Review access controls before connecting them.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies across the integration.
